For example, ice cream sells for more on a hot summer day because more people want it. Sellers and buyers together find a price that works for both.

Supply and demand is a model of microeconomics. It describes how a price is formed in a market economy. There are two determining factors on such a market, the number of things made available, called supply, and the number of things consumers want, called demand. Supply and demand shows how producers and consumers interact with each other. This relationship will fix the price for a certain type of good.  In perfect competition, the quantity demanded (demand) and the quantity supplied will be equal.  This happens at the equilibrium market price.

A telescope is a tool that makes faraway things look closer and bigger. Astronomers use telescopes to study the Moon, planets, stars, and galaxies. Some telescopes use curved pieces of glass, called lenses, to bend the light and focus it. Others use curved mirrors to collect light. The bigger the telescope is, the more light it can gather, and the fainter the objects it can show. Some telescopes are even sent into space, because the air around Earth can blur the view.

A telescope (from the Ancient Greek τῆλε, tele "far" and σκοπεῖν, skopein "to look or see"; τηλεσκόπος, teleskopos) makes astronomical objects appear closer to the naked eye. It is an important tool for astronomy that gathers light and directs it to a single point. Some do this with curved mirrors, some with curved lenses, and some with both. Telescopes make distant things look bigger, brighter and closer. Galileo was the first person to use a telescope for astronomy, but he did not invent them. The first telescope was invented in the Netherlands in 1608. Some telescopes, not mainly used for astronomy, are binoculars, camera lenses, or spyglasses.

A vaccine is a medicine that helps your body learn how to fight a germ before you ever get sick from it. A vaccine contains a weak or dead piece of the germ, or a small part of it. It cannot make you ill, but your body sees it and builds defenses. Later, if the real germ enters your body, your immune system remembers it and can fight it off quickly. Vaccines have helped stop serious diseases like polio and measles from spreading to many people.

One common type of vaccine is a "live vaccine."  This type of vaccine contains a small amount of a live virus or bacteria.  Before the vaccine is given, scientists weaken the virus or bacteria so it cannot make a person sick.  When a person gets a live vaccine, their immune system learns to recognize and fight off that virus or bacteria.  Then, if the person is exposed to the virus or bacteria in the future, their immune system will already "know" how to fight it off.  Examples of live vaccines include vaccines for measles, mumps, and chickenpox.

A volcano is an opening in the Earth's surface where hot melted rock, called magma, can escape. Deep underground, it is so hot that rock melts. When pressure builds up, the magma rises and bursts out as lava, ash, and gas. Over time, the lava cools and hardens, building up a mountain shape around the opening. Some volcanoes erupt often, while others stay quiet for hundreds of years. Volcanoes can be dangerous, but their ash also makes soil rich and good for growing crops.

The world's biggest volcano is named Mauna Loa in Hawaii. Mauna Loa is part of the five volcanoes on Hawaii's 'Big Island'. The most recent time this volcano erupted was in 1984. It erupted 33 times in the last 170 years. Like all the other Hawaiian volcanoes, Mauna Loa was created by the movement of the Pacific tectonic plate which moved over the Hawaii hotspot in the Earth's mantle. Mauna Loa is 4,196 meters tall. It is a shield volcano. The largest recent eruption from Mauna Loa left a lava trail  long.

A web browser is a program that lets you visit websites. Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge are all web browsers. When you type an address into the browser or click a link, it asks a computer far away, called a server, to send the page. The browser then takes the code it receives and turns it into the pictures, text, and buttons that you see on your screen. Browsers also keep a list of your bookmarks and history, and they have settings that help protect your privacy.

Web browsers are used by people to find and look at websites on the Internet. The first web browser was created in 1990. Many web browsers are available for free. All web browsers can go to websites but each browser has good things and bad things about it. For example, some browsers focus on data security and keeping computers safe from viruses. Other browsers are made so that web pages appear on-screen faster.

Assignment statements are used to bind names to values and to modify attributes or items of mutable objects. When a target is a simple name, the name is bound to the object produced by evaluating the right-hand side in the current namespace. If the target is an attribute reference, the object's attribute is set, and if it is a subscription, the container's item assignment method is invoked. In chained assignment, the expression is evaluated once and then assigned to each target from left to right.

Assignment is defined recursively depending on the form of the target (list). When a target is part of a mutable object (an attribute reference, subscription or slicing), the mutable object must ultimately perform the assignment and decide about its validity, and may raise an exception if the assignment is unacceptable. The rules observed by various types and the exceptions raised are given with the definition of the object types (see section The standard type hierarchy).

The binary arithmetic operators have the conventional priority levels. The multiplication operator yields the product of its arguments, which must either both be numbers or one must be an integer and the other a sequence. In the latter case, the sequence is repeated that many times. The division operators yield the quotient of their arguments, and dividing by zero raises a ZeroDivisionError exception. The modulo operator yields the remainder of the division of the first argument by the second.

The "*" (multiplication) operator yields the product of its arguments. The arguments must either both be numbers, or one argument must be an integer and the other must be a sequence. In the former case, the numbers are converted to a common type and then multiplied together. In the latter case, sequence repetition is performed; a negative repetition factor yields an empty sequence.

A class definition is an executable statement that creates a new class object. The inheritance list, if present, is evaluated first and normally gives a list of base classes. The class body is then executed in a new namespace, and when the body finishes, its namespace is passed to the metaclass, which constructs the class. Finally, the resulting class object is bound to the class name in the enclosing scope. Decorators, if specified, are applied to the class after it has been created.

The class's suite is then executed in a new execution frame (see Naming and binding), using a newly created local namespace and the original global namespace. (Usually, the suite contains mostly function definitions.) When the class's suite finishes execution, its execution frame is discarded but its local namespace is saved. [5] A class object is then created using the inheritance list for the base classes and the saved local namespace for the attribute dictionary. The class name is bound to this class object in the original local namespace.

Comparison operators can be chained arbitrarily, so that an expression such as x < y <= z is equivalent to x < y and y <= z, except that y is evaluated only once. If the first comparison is false, the remaining comparisons are not evaluated. The equality operators compare the values of two objects, whereas the identity operators test whether two names refer to exactly the same object. Objects of different types, except for different numeric types, never compare equal by default.

Chapter Objects, values and types states that objects have a value (in addition to type and identity). The value of an object is a rather abstract notion in Python: For example, there is no canonical access method for an object's value. Also, there is no requirement that the value of an object should be constructed in a particular way, e.g. comprised of all its data attributes. Comparison operators implement a particular notion of what the value of an object is. One can think of them as defining the value of an object indirectly, by means of their comparison implementation.

Compound statements contain groups of other statements and affect or control the execution of those other statements in some way. A compound statement consists of one or more clauses, each of which has a header and a suite. The header begins with a unique keyword and ends with a colon, and the suite is the group of statements controlled by the clause. A suite can be a set of statements on the same line as the header or one or more indented statements on subsequent lines.

It selects exactly one of the suites by evaluating the expressions one by one until one is found to be true (see section Boolean operations for the definition of true and false); then that suite is executed (and no other part of the "if" statement is executed or evaluated). If all expressions are false, the suite of the "else" clause, if present, is executed.

A context manager is an object that defines the runtime context to be entered and exited around a block of code. It is invoked by the with statement, which calls the object's enter method before the suite is executed and its exit method afterward. The exit method receives information about any exception raised in the suite, and if it returns a true value, the exception is suppressed. Context managers are commonly used to ensure that resources such as files and locks are released reliably.

A *context manager* is an object that defines the runtime context to be established when executing a "with" statement. The context manager handles the entry into, and the exit from, the desired runtime context for the execution of the block of code. Context managers are normally invoked using the "with" statement (described in section The with statement), but can also be used by directly invoking their methods.

Classes can customize the behavior of built-in operations by defining special methods. The rich comparison methods, for example, correspond to the six comparison operators and are called to implement them. Each method receives the other operand and may return any value, though a Boolean is typical. If a method does not support the operation for the given operands, it should return the NotImplemented singleton, which signals the interpreter to try the reflected operation on the other operand.

A rich comparison method may return the singleton "NotImplemented" if it does not implement the operation for a given pair of arguments. By convention, "False" and "True" are returned for a successful comparison. However, these methods can return any value, so if the comparison operator is used in a Boolean context (e.g., in the condition of an "if" statement), Python will call "bool()" on the value to determine if the result is true or false.

Python ships with an interactive debugger, pdb, that lets you pause a running program and look around. You can place breakpoints at chosen lines, advance one statement at a time, print variables, and move up and down the call stack to see how a function was reached. Calling the built-in breakpoint function in your code starts the debugger at that spot. If a program crashes, you can also start the debugger afterward and examine the state at the moment of failure.

The module "pdb" defines an interactive source code debugger for Python programs. It supports setting (conditional) breakpoints and single stepping at the source line level, inspection of stack frames, source code listing, and evaluation of arbitrary Python code in the context of any stack frame. It also supports post-mortem debugging and can be called under program control.

Dictionaries map keys to values and are written with curly braces containing key and value pairs. Looking up a key is fast, because the key is hashed to locate its entry directly. Only hashable objects, such as strings, numbers, and tuples of immutable items, can serve as keys, whereas lists cannot. When the same key is written twice in one literal, the later pair silently replaces the earlier one. Since Python 3.7, dictionaries also remember the order in which keys were inserted.

If a comma-separated sequence of dict items is given, they are evaluated from left to right to define the entries of the dictionary: each key object is used as a key into the dictionary to store the corresponding value. This means that you can specify the same key multiple times in the dict item list, and the final dictionary's value for that key will be the last one given.

Because Python resolves most names dynamically, several built-in functions allow code to be constructed and executed at runtime. The eval function evaluates an expression string, while the exec function executes a string containing statements. Both accept optional dictionaries that serve as the global and local namespaces for the evaluated code. If these arguments are omitted, the code is executed in the current namespace. Such features should be used with caution, particularly with untrusted input.

The "eval()" and "exec()" functions do not have access to the full environment for resolving names. Names may be resolved in the local and global namespaces of the caller. Free variables are not resolved in the nearest enclosing namespace, but in the global namespace. [1] The "exec()" and "eval()" functions have optional arguments to override the global and local namespace. If only one namespace is specified, it is used for both.

Exceptions provide a mechanism for transferring control out of the normal flow of a program when an error or other exceptional condition occurs. An exception is raised explicitly by the raise statement or implicitly by the interpreter when an operation fails. The try statement specifies exception handlers for a block of code, and the first matching except clause handles the exception. If no handler is found in the current frame, the exception propagates up the call stack until it is caught or terminates the program.

Exceptions are a means of breaking out of the normal flow of control of a code block in order to handle errors or other exceptional conditions. An exception is *raised* at the point where the error is detected; it may be *handled* by the surrounding code block or by any code block that directly or indirectly invoked the code block where the error occurred.

Python programs are built from code blocks, and each block has its own scope for names. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local to that function unless a global or nonlocal declaration says otherwise. When a name is used, the interpreter looks in the local scope, then in any enclosing function scopes, then in the module's global scope, and finally in the built-in names. This lookup order is determined by the program text, not by the order in which calls happen at runtime.

If a name is bound in a block, it is a local variable of that block, unless declared as "nonlocal" or "global". If a name is bound at the module level, it is a global variable. (The variables of the module code block are local and global.) If a variable is used in a code block but not defined there, it is a *free variable*.

The for statement is used to iterate over the elements of a sequence or other iterable object. The expression list is evaluated once and must yield an iterable object, from which an iterator is created. The suite is then executed once for each item provided by the iterator, with the target list assigned the item in turn. When the items are exhausted, the optional else clause is executed, unless the loop was terminated by a break statement.

The "starred_list" expression is evaluated once; it should yield an *iterable* object. An *iterator* is created for that iterable. The first item provided by the iterator is then assigned to the target list using the standard rules for assignments (see Assignment statements), and the suite is executed. This repeats for each item provided by the iterator. When the iterator is exhausted, the suite in the "else" clause, if present, is executed, and the loop terminates.

The format string syntax uses replacement fields surrounded by curly braces. Anything that is not contained in braces is treated as literal text and copied unchanged to the output. A replacement field begins with an optional field name that specifies the object whose value is to be formatted, followed by an optional conversion and an optional format specification introduced by a colon. Literal braces can be included in the output by doubling them.

In less formal terms, the replacement field can start with a *field_name* that specifies the object whose value is to be formatted and inserted into the output instead of the replacement field. The *field_name* is optionally followed by a *conversion* field, which is preceded by an exclamation point "'!'", and a *format_spec*, which is preceded by a colon "':'". These specify a non-default format for the replacement value.

A function definition is an executable statement that creates a function object and binds it to the function name in the current local namespace. The function body is not executed at definition time, but only when the function is called. Parameters can have default values, which are evaluated once, from left to right, when the function is defined. For this reason, using a mutable object such as a list as a default value can lead to unexpected behavior across calls.

When one or more *parameters* have the form *parameter* "=" *expression*, the function is said to have "default parameter values." For a parameter with a default value, the corresponding *argument* may be omitted from a call, in which case the parameter's default value is substituted. If a parameter has a default value, all following parameters up until the ""*"" must also have a default value — this is a syntactic restriction that is not expressed by the grammar.

The import statement is executed in two steps: first it finds and loads the module, and then it binds the results to a name in the local namespace. If the requested module is not found in the module cache, the import system searches for it using a sequence of finders, which consult the entries of the module search path. Once loaded, the module object is stored in the cache so that subsequent imports of the same name return the same object.

The details of the first step, finding and loading modules, are described in greater detail in the section on the import system, which also describes the various types of packages and modules that can be imported, as well as all the hooks that can be used to customize the import system. Note that failures in this step may indicate either that the module could not be located, *or* that an error occurred while initializing the module, which includes execution of the module's code.

Lists are ordered, mutable collections that can hold items of any type, including other lists. They are created with square brackets, either by writing the items out separated by commas or by using a comprehension that builds the contents from an iterable. Because lists are mutable, their items can be replaced, appended, or removed after creation, and several names may refer to the same list object. Indexing starts at zero, negative indices count from the end, and slicing returns a new list containing a copy of the selected range.

A list display yields a new list object, the contents being specified by either a list of expressions or a comprehension. When a comma- separated list of expressions is supplied, its elements are evaluated from left to right and placed into the list object in that order. When a comprehension is supplied, the list is constructed from the elements resulting from the comprehension.

Every object has an identity, a type, and a value. The identity of an object never changes once it has been created, and it can be thought of as the object's address in memory. An object's type determines the operations that it supports and the possible values it can hold. Objects whose value can change are said to be mutable, while objects whose value cannot change once they are created are called immutable. Lists and dictionaries are mutable, whereas tuples and strings are immutable.

The *value* of some objects can change. Objects whose value can change are said to be *mutable*; objects whose value is unchangeable once they are created are called *immutable*. (The value of an immutable container object that contains a reference to a mutable object can change when the latter's value is changed; however the container is still considered immutable, because the collection of objects it contains cannot be changed. So, immutability is not strictly the same as having an unchangeable value, it is more subtle.) An object's mutability is determined by its type; for instance, numbers, strings and tuples are immutable, while dictionaries and lists are mutable.

A class can emulate a sequence type by implementing the methods that the interpreter calls for container operations. The subscription method is called to evaluate an item lookup, and for sequence types the accepted keys should be integers and slice objects. Negative indices are typically handled by the method itself, and it should raise an IndexError for values outside the range of the sequence. Implementing the length method allows the built-in len function to work with the object.

Called to implement evaluation of "self[key]". For *sequence* types, the accepted keys should be integers. Optionally, they may support "slice" objects as well. Negative index support is also optional. If *key* is of an inappropriate type, "TypeError" may be raised; if *key* is a value outside the set of indexes for the sequence (after any special interpretation of negative values), "IndexError" should be raised. For *mapping* types, if *key* is missing (not in the container), "KeyError" should be raised.

A slicing selects a range of items in a sequence object, such as a string, tuple, or list. Slicings may be used as expressions or as targets in assignment statements. The syntax consists of a primary followed by a square-bracketed slice list. A simple slice specifies a lower bound, an upper bound, and an optional stride, separated by colons. The resulting object has the same type as the original, and omitted bounds default to the beginning and end of the sequence.

There is ambiguity in the formal syntax here: anything that looks like an expression list also looks like a slice list, so any subscription can be interpreted as a slicing. Rather than further complicating the syntax, this is disambiguated by defining that in this case the interpretation as a subscription takes priority over the interpretation as a slicing (this is the case if the slice list contains no proper slice).
